newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Opposition attacks Yeltsin, says Russia leaderless.
newsitem.headline: Opposition attacks Yeltsin, says Russia leaderless.

text.p: Opposition leaders, addressing parliament's first full session since President Boris Yeltsin announced he would have heart surgery, said on Wednesday Russia was leaderless and demanded action to stop the rot.

"If the car is smashed up and the driver is in hospital, you should change the car and the driver," extreme nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky told the opposition-dominated State Duma, the lower house, at the start of its autumn session.

He and other opposition leaders painted a picture of chaos and confusion in Yeltsin's absence, sharpening their knives for what promises to be an autumn of battles with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government and the Kremlin.

Yeltsin's chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais hit back, telling a news conference the president was in control. "I don't know of a situation when we needed a presidential decision in some difficult, dramatic conflict and we weren't able to get it."

But Chubais, who said he had not seen the president since last week, acknowledged that Yeltsin's limited working time of two to three hours a day was not ideal and took a swipe at one of his own rivals, ambitious security chief Alexander Lebed.
Yeltsin, 65, announced on September 5 that he would have a heart operation and has been in hospital since September 13.
His bypass surgery is due in six to 10 weeks time and the chief of the presidential medical centre said on Wednesday that doctors were satisfied with the latest medical tests.
Chubais unveiled a new-look Kremlin administration and said the changes he had undertaken since Yeltsin's reelection in July meant the president's orders would be obeyed.
"Officials should not discuss orders but carry them out," said Chubais, the 41-year-old former economic reform supremo who helped engineer Yeltsin's election victory.
Yeltsin met Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the Middle East and Afghanistan.

A proposal by Yeltsin for the 12-member Commonwealth of Independent States, set up on the ashes of the Soviet Union in 1991, to discuss the situation in Afghanistan bore fruit. The meeting was expected to go ahead in Kazakhstan on Friday.
The president also sent a message to the Duma asking for "significantly" better and more intensive work.

Previous sessions have been marred by fights between deputies, battles of will with Yeltsin and the passing of few laws, and Thursday is the third anniversary of a rebellion by the old parliament which Yeltsin put down with tanks.

At the opening session, Lebed came under fierce fire for his efforts to forge a peace deal in rebel Chechnya from deputies on both sides of the chamber as well as Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov who accused him of capitulating to the rebels.
Parliamentarians cried "Shame, Shame" and "Traitor" as Lebed tried to explain that the deal did not jeapoardise Russia's territorial integrity.

The fierce abuse came on the eve of a new round of peace talks in Moscow. Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, due to arrive on Thursday, was sticking by demands for Chechen independence, Interfax news agency said.

The new parliamentary session is likely to be dominated by a struggle with the government over its budget plans, which need Duma approval to become law, and by demands for the government to pay off months of unpaid wages to millions of workers.
Deputies laid down the gauntlet by inviting Chernomyrdin to address the Duma on the social and economic situation on Friday.
The prime minister, who has resisted calls to loosen purse strings to cut inflation and satisfy foreign creditors, says matters are in hand and has refused similar demands in the past.

"The government is unable to resolve a single question," said Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, who heads the most powerful opposition force. "If things go on like this Russia will repeat the fate of the Soviet Union."
Zyuganov proposed a Council of State be set up, grouping leaders of the main political and national security bodies, to examine the country's problems and decide what should be done.
But Chubais said that it was too early to look beyond Yeltsin's term and said Chernomyrdin was working hard, just not seeking the limelight like Lebed.
